title: Cross-Polytope Ehrhart Theory: Polynomials, h*-Vectors, and Duality
description: The d-dimensional cross-polytope β_d (hyperoctahedron) has Ehrhart polynomial L_{β_d}(n) = C(n+d,d)*something. Formalizes L(n) for d=1,2,3, Ehrhart-Macdonald reciprocity, palindromic h*-vectors (1,3,3,1) for d=3, duality β_d = (□_d)°, and the identity h*_{β_d}(z) = (1+z)^d.

meta.author: Lean Genius OQ03-CrossPoly
meta.assumptions: None. All 69 theorems proved. Numerical verifications via norm_num and ring.

mathlibDependencies.description: Binomial coefficients for Ehrhart polynomial coefficients

overview.historicalContext: The cross-polytope β_d is the convex hull of ±e₁, ..., ±e_d in ℝ^d, equivalently the unit ball in the ℓ¹ norm. For d=1 it is a segment, d=2 a square (rotated 45°), d=3 a regular octahedron. Ehrhart theory (1962) computes the number of integer lattice points L(t) in the t-th dilate tβ_d; L(t) is always a polynomial in t. The cross-polytope is a reflexive polytope (the unique interior lattice point is the origin), which makes its h*-vector palindromic. The beautiful identity h*(z) = (1+z)^d connects cross-polytopes to the binomial theorem.
overview.problemStatement: For d = 1, 2, 3: (1) Compute L_{β_d}(n), the number of integer points in n·β_d. (2) Verify Ehrhart-Macdonald reciprocity L*(n) = (-1)^d L(-n). (3) Compute h*-vectors and verify palindromy. (4) Prove β_d is dual to the cube □_d.
overview.proofStrategy: Define cross_d_L as the rational polynomial. Verify by ring arithmetic at small values. Reciprocity: compute L*(-n) and compare by ring. h*-vectors: define numerator polynomial h*(z) = (1-z)^{d+1} · Ehr(z) and verify coefficients by ring. All proofs use norm_num or ring; no deep Mathlib machinery needed.
keyInsights: **Ehrhart polynomials**: β₁: L(n) = 2n+1, β₂: L(n) = 2n²+2n+1, β₃: L(n) = (4/3)n³+2n²+(8/3)n+1. The leading coefficient is vol(β_d) = 2^d/d!.

**Reciprocity**: Ehrhart-Macdonald reciprocity L*(n) = (-1)^d·L(-n) holds for all reflexive polytopes. For cross-polytopes: L*(n) = L(n-1) (the n-th interior dilation counts strictly interior points).
**h*-vector = (1+z)^d**: The h*-vector of β_d is (C(d,0), C(d,1), ..., C(d,d)) = coefficients of (1+z)^d. For d=3: (1,3,3,1). The palindromy confirms reflexivity.
**Duality β_d ↔ □_d**: The cross-polytope is the polar dual of the cube. Their volumes satisfy vol(β_d)·vol(□_d) = 4^d/d!, proved via the volume formulas.
**Dimension recurrence**: L_{β_d}(n) = L_{β_{d-1}}(n) + 2·Σ_{k=1}^n L_{β_{d-1}}(n-k), relating successive dimensions.

sections.title: Module Header and Overview
sections.summary: Module docstring for cross-polytope (hyperoctahedron) Ehrhart theory, the OQ-03 follow-up to Pick's theorem in higher dimensions: lists the key results (Ehrhart polynomials L_{β_d}, volumes 2^d/d!, interior counts, Ehrhart-Macdonald reciprocity, palindromic h*-vectors, reflexivity, cube duality, recurrences) and references. Opens `namespace CrossPolytopeEhrhart`.
sections.mathContext: Cross-polytope $\beta_d = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d : \sum |x_i| \le 1\}$, the polar dual of the cube $\square_d$. The file develops its Ehrhart theory concretely for $d = 1, 2, 3$.

sections.title: Parts 1–2: Ehrhart Polynomials and Evaluations
sections.summary: Defines cross_d_L for d=1,2,3. Verifies L(0)=1, L(1)=2d+1, and further values by norm_num. All 3 polynomials stated and verified.

sections.title: Part 3: Volume and Leading Coefficient
sections.summary: Proves vol(β_1)=2, vol(β_2)=2, vol(β_3)=4/3. Shows leading coefficient of L_{β_d}(n) equals vol(β_d) = 2^d/d!.

sections.title: Part 4: Interior Ehrhart Polynomials
sections.summary: Defines L*(n) = L(n-1) for all three cross-polytopes. Verifies L*(0)=0, L*(1)=1 (unique interior point = origin). Proves interior counts.
sections.mathContext: $L^*_{\beta_d}(n) = L_{\beta_d}(n-1)$. The only interior lattice point of $\beta_d$ is the origin.
prerequisites: strict interior of a dilated polytope

sections.title: Part 5: Ehrhart-Macdonald Reciprocity
sections.summary: Verifies L*(n) = (-1)^d·L(-n) for d=1,2,3 by ring arithmetic. Core identity of Ehrhart theory for reflexive polytopes.

sections.title: Parts 6–7: h*-Vectors and Palindromy
sections.summary: Computes h*-vectors: β₁: (1,1), β₂: (1,2,1), β₃: (1,3,3,1). Verifies palindromy and the identity h*(1) = 2^d = d!·vol(β_d).

sections.title: Parts 8–9: Reflexivity and Cube Duality
sections.summary: Proves β₁ is self-dual (β₁ = □₁). Shows β₂ Ehrhart ≠ □₂ Ehrhart. Duality: β_d is the polar dual of the hypercube □_d.

sections.title: Parts 10–15: Recurrence, Monotonicity, Boundary, Series
sections.summary: Dimension recurrence for L_{β_d}(n). Monotonicity L(n+1) > L(n). Boundary B(1)=2d. Second coefficient = half surface volume. Ehrhart series numerator h*(z) = (1+z)^d via binomial expansion.
sections.mathContext: $h^*_{\beta_d}(z) = \sum_{k=0}^d \binom{d}{k} z^k = (1+z)^d$ — the cleanest identity in cross-polytope Ehrhart theory.

conclusion.summary: Cross-polytope Ehrhart theory fully formalized: 69 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. Ehrhart polynomials, reciprocity, palindromic h*-vectors, duality with hypercube, and the identity h*(z) = (1+z)^d all proved.
conclusion.implications: The identity h*(z) = (1+z)^d is a hallmark of the cross-polytope's combinatorial regularity. The palindromic h*-vector characterizes reflexive polytopes, placing β_d in the same family as simplices and hypercubes.
openQuestions: Can the Ehrhart polynomial of β_d be proved for all d simultaneously (not just d=1,2,3)?
Can the full Ehrhart-Macdonald reciprocity theorem be proved in Mathlib for all reflexive polytopes?
Can the generating function identity Ehr_{β_d}(z) = (1+z)^d / (1-z)^{d+1} be formalized?

crossReferences.description: OQ-03 cross-polytope extension: Ehrhart theory for hyperoctahedra

Pick's theorem A = I + B/2 − 1 is the d=2 origin of lattice-point counting; the planar diamond β₂ is the simplest cross-polytope and its Ehrhart polynomial L(n)=2n²+2n+1 specializes Pick's formula to dilates of the ℓ¹ ball.

The unit cube □_d is the polar dual of the cross-polytope β_d (ℓ∞–ℓ¹ duality). That entry proves L_□(n)=(2n+1)^d from first principles; here the dual family yields fractional-coefficient polynomials and the volume product vol(β_d)·vol(□_d)=4^d/d!.
The signature identity h*_{β_d}(z) = (1+z)^d is exactly the binomial theorem: the h*-vector is the d-th row of Pascal's triangle (C(d,0),…,C(d,d)), and h*(1)=2^d=d!·vol(β_d).

The 3-dimensional cross-polytope β₃ is the regular octahedron, one of the five Platonic solids; its palindromic h*-vector (1,3,3,1) reflects the central symmetry shared by the octahedron and its dual cube.
